contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned to see systems. Today: a standard framework for evaluating whether a system is actually sustainable.

Sustainability is commonly analyzed through three connected pillars: environmental (does it protect ecosystems and natural resources?), economic (is it financially viable over time?), and social (does it meet human needs fairly?). A genuinely sustainable solution addresses all three — a plan that's environmentally sound but economically unworkable won't last, and one that's profitable but environmentally destructive isn't truly sustainable either. For example, a farm using water-efficient irrigation (environmental) that also costs less to run long-term (economic) and provides stable local jobs (social) addresses all three pillars together. Choose one real environmental issue you're aware of and briefly analyze it through all three pillars.

You now have a real, standard framework for evaluating sustainability, not just an intuitive sense of 'good for the environment.' Tomorrow we'll look at feedback loops specifically within environmental systems.

objectives: Define the three pillars of sustainability: environmental, economic, social
Analyze a real environmental issue through all three pillars
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's systems-thinking framework.
2. Introduce the three pillars using the water-efficient irrigation example.
3. Discuss why addressing only one or two pillars often isn't truly sustainable.
4. Have the child choose a real issue and analyze it through all three pillars.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's topic: feedback loops in environmental systems.
differentiationTips: Struggling: provide one pre-selected environmental issue (like recycling programs or public transit) to analyze rather than requiring the child to choose their own
Ready for more: ask them to identify a real example where addressing only one or two pillars caused a solution to fail or be criticized
Keep this lesson at the general framework level — specific policy debates are out of scope here
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. The three pillars are environmental, economic, and social. 2. A genuinely sustainable solution addresses all three — for example, water-efficient irrigation that's also affordable long-term and supports stable local jobs.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'sustainability' description, establishing the standard three-pillars framework used throughout environmental science and policy analysis.
